A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Low density steel
Deformation induced transformation
Thermomechanical processing
Thermodynamic modelling
A B S T R A C T
The Gibbs energy model as an effective thermodynamic function along with detailed microstructural analyses
were employed to assess the capability of strain induced transformations in a ferrite based lightweight steel. In
this respect, the material was deformed in a warm temperature regime in compression mode and the resultant
microstructures were studied in details. The progressive and extensive development of the banded structure was
led to the partitioning of the ferrite phase and also the shearing of the parent austenite. The shear strain
localization was effectively released through simultaneous transformation of ferrite to austenite and austenite to
ferrite transformations as an effective strain compensation mechanism. This was led to appreciable flow soft
ening in corresponding flow curves. The capability for bidirectional transformation resulted from the specified
local elemental partitioning of Al and Mn and the resultant exactly same levels of Gibbs energies of each con
stituent phases.
1. Introduction
Various deformation mechanisms: (i) cell-structure formation and
substructure development [1], (ii) short-range ordering and formation of
Taylor lattice structure [2], (iii) micro-shear band induced plasticity [3,
4], and (iv) slip band refinement and grain subdivision [2,5], have been
proposed to justify the high capability of low density steels for dynamic
strain hardening. These specified micro-mechanisms are exceptional
ways for strain compensation which finally results in outstanding
strength/ductility balances [6,7]. Interestingly, the nano-precipitation
of kappa phase has been also introduced as an effective strain accom
modation mechanism [8].
Another aspect which has been mainly overlooked in previous re
searches is the capability of lightweight steels for the occurrence of
dynamic transformation in the course of straining. Owing to the high
stacking fault energy of low density steels (80–110 mJ/m<sup>2</sup>), the
austenite to martensite transformation is theoretically impossible and
the transformation induced plasticity effect is disregarded, however, the
probability of deformation induced austenite to ferrite and ferrite to
austenite transformations should be re-considered. In this respect, the
thermodynamic interpretation of the microstructural evolution is
introduced as an effective solution, and the “modified Gibbs energy
model” can be successfully employed to interpret the kinetic of phase
transformation in multicomponent alloying systems [9]. Such approach
has been previously applied in the case of low carbon steels [10] and
advanced high strength steels [11], just for confirming the experimental
results [12].
In the case of lightweight steels, the microstructural evolutions seem
to be more complex, and the effects of alloying element and their par
titioning effects on the phase stability and stress/strain induced trans
formations [13], phase fraction and phase distribution [14] are more
prominent. In this respect, the role of thermodynamic interpretation
combined with detailed microstructural analysis should be over
emphasized; this is highly necessitated for successful alloy designing
[15] and results in a compromise between the manufacturing costs and

The strain within the ferrite is mainly accommodated through acti

high dislocation density walls (HDDWs) can be traced through the

within the ferrite phase at this relatively low temperature seems to be
reasonable. The dislocation configuration in austenite was quite
different at the same imposed strain of 0.3, as it is observed in Fig. 3b.

5 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }

and d, where the banded structure is clearly revealed by dashed-black
ovals. As it can be realized, the parent austenite has been effectively
sheared through the propagation of the deformation bands. Interest
ingly, the simultaneous occurrence of the deformation induced “ferrite
to austenite” and “austenite to ferrite” transformations are recognized
along with the deformation bands which are depicted by red and green
arrows, respectively. In fact, the shear strain localization along the
deformation bands is released through the transformation of the
austenite to ferrite or ferrite to austenite as an effective emerging strain
compensation mechanism. Such capability of the material for
transformation-based strain accommodation reduces the flow localiza
tion’s effect, causes flow softening and increases the workability of the
experimented material. The occurrence of deformation induced ferrite
transformation has been previously reported in the case of Fe–Mn–Al–C
alloys at higher temperatures where the probability of such trans
formation is theoretically reasonable [3]. However, in the present case,
the simultaneous occurrence of deformation-induced ferrite trans
formation (DIFT) and deformation-induced austenite transformation
(DIAT) at such a low temperature regime seems phenomenal and needs
to be well clarified. It would be necessary to mention that such trans
formations can’t be characterized in the microstructures which have
been deformed at higher temperature of 600 <sup>◦</sup>C (see Fig. 3e).

In this respect, the partitioning of Mn and Al elements as the function
of temperature in the constituent phases are represented in Fig. 4a–b.
Different phases are predicted by Thermo-Calc in both diagrams: (1)
BCC_A2 and (2) FCC_A1 (Face Centered Cubic) represent the ferrite and
austenite phase in order. Furthermore, (3) BCC_A1#2 is a phase with the
BCC structure which owns an extremely high amount of Mn. Addition
ally, both Mn and Al partitioned into ferrite and austenite. As it is ex
pected, Mn has been partitioned more in austenite and also Al in ferrite.

regime, many dislocations were tangled to form the cell structures
within the ferrite and a planar slip-like character was formed. The fre-
quency of slip bands was noticeable and formation/intersection of them
was led to development of banded structure. The parent austenite was
also effectively sheared through the propagation of these banded
structure. Shear strain localization along the deformation bands was
released through the simultaneous transformation of the austenite to
ferrite or ferrite to austenite as an effective emerging strain compensa
tion mechanism. This resulted in reduction of flow localization’s effect,
caused flow softening and increased the workability of the experimented
material. Bidirectional transformation was justified from thermody
namic point of view considering the exactly same level of Gibbs energy
for both ferrite and austenite as a consequence of Al/Mn elemental
partitioning.
